claims.claim: **Common and benign**: it affects the cosmetic appearance of the head and **does not cause developmental delay.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No imaging is required**: diagnose on history and examination, including the absence of craniosynostosis features. Cranial X-ray or CT is not needed to confirm plagiocephaly or brachycephaly.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Look for a co-existing tight sternocleidomastoid** (congenital muscular torticollis) and other risk factors.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Most resolve without treatment**, improving with counterpositioning and physiotherapy.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Positional plagiocephaly** = posterior flattening on one side, possibly with ear misalignment and facial asymmetry. **Brachycephaly** = symmetrical occipital flattening and widening, often co-existing. **Scaphocephaly** = long narrow skull flattened on both sides.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Caused by external moulding** from lying on the back or a one-sided posture preference. **Risk factors:** little tummy time, low tone, tight SCM, delayed gross motor development, developmental dysplasia of the hip.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **More than a third of infants** develop plagiocephaly during their first months; most **self-correct by the time they can sit unsupported**, thanks to fast cranial growth over the first 4–6 months (corrected age if premature).
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Plagiocephaly and brachycephaly persist in around 1% of teenagers.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Craniosynostosis** = premature fusion of one or more sutures with **ridging**; it may affect brain development, **does not improve over time**, and can be syndromic (e.g. Apert, Crouzon).
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mimics:** unilateral coronal craniosynostosis (forehead flattening) and unilateral lambdoid craniosynostosis (occipital flattening opposite the forehead protuberance).
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Congenital muscular torticollis**, usually noted in the first month: head tilt toward the tight SCM, looking to the opposite side, plagiocephaly on the opposite side, sometimes a palpable SCM lump.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Identify torticollis early and refer to a physiotherapist** — plagiocephaly improves once the tight SCM is treated. Also associated: reduced vision or nystagmus (head tilt to see more clearly) and cervical scoliosis, e.g. Klippel-Feil syndrome.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Assess for plagiocephaly** with any of: head-turning preference, head tilt, one-sided posterior flattening (parents may report a bump on the 'normal' side), symmetrical occipital flattening, ear displacement, forehead asymmetry, facial asymmetry.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **History:** birth (breech, multiple) and gestation; one-sided looking preference awake and asleep; gross motor development and tolerance of tummy time; handling, sleeping, feeding and carrying positions; change in head shape over time.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine from above**, infant on the parent's lap: a **parallelogram-shaped head**, frontal protuberance and forward ear on the side of the flattening, and a posterior bump on the opposite side support plagiocephaly.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Palpate the anterior fontanelle:** closed in 1% at 3 months, 38% at 12 months and 96% at 24 months. **An open fontanelle predicts better response** to physiotherapy or helmet therapy.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Feel for ridging of the coronal or sagittal sutures** (craniosynostosis), and examine the back and spine, eye movements, head circumference and neurology.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Suspected craniosynostosis → urgent referral to a craniofacial service**, which decides on imaging.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **No pillow of any kind in sleep**, whether to prevent or to treat flattening — **risk of sudden infant death syndrome.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Counterpositioning:** reduce time on the flat side by arranging the environment so the infant turns toward the opposite side.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Example, right-sided plagiocephaly:** move the cot so the infant looks left when a carer enters; lay on the left side or back with toys on the left; carry to encourage turning left. **Regular tummy time** builds neck strength and head control.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Physiotherapy:** parent education, handling and counterpositioning advice, and — for congenital muscular torticollis — passive stretches of the opposite SCM plus strengthening of it; the physiotherapist also monitors progress and advises on specialist referral.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Some evidence supports a helmet for severe deformity not improving** with counterpositioning and physiotherapy; **some residual deformity remains** even with a helmet.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Optimal timing is around 6–7 months**; infants with developmental delay or torticollis may qualify with less deformity. **Unlikely to help after 10 months.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Custom-made by an orthotist and worn 23 hours a day**, for an average of 6 weeks to 3 months. For brachycephaly it prevents further widening but does not reverse it.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Severity scales** (e.g. 0 = no asymmetry to 3 = severe, per feature) guide referral and monitoring; **helmet thresholds vary — seek local specialist advice.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refer to a specialist clinic** (paediatrics or craniofacial) for: severe head shape worsening despite counterpositioning and physiotherapy · suspected craniosynostosis · congenital muscular torticollis not improving with community physiotherapy.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23
